section.title: Chapter review and discovery problems
section.p: This chapter began with a simple observation:
section.md: f'(x)>0 \text{ means rising}, \qquad f'(x)<0 \text{ means falling}.
section.p: That observation grew into a much larger picture. The derivative gives more than instantaneous rate. It gives shape, turning, bending, bounds, and sometimes limits.

subsection.title: The chapter’s map
subsection.p: Here is the main dictionary.

md.mrow: f'(c)=0 \text{ or } f'(c)\text{ undefined} \amp c \text{ is a critical number candidate}
f'' \text{ changes sign at } c \amp (c,f(c)) \text{ is an inflection point}

exercise.title: How does derivative evidence become graph information?

statement.p: The chapter’s map translates signs of f' and f'' into rising, falling, concavity, extrema, and inflection. In your own words, why is that dictionary more than a list of tests, and what single idea lets local rate information describe the shape of a graph?

hint.p: The first derivative is about direction of change; the second is about how that direction itself is changing. Sign charts are a way of reading those stories across intervals.

exercise.title: Why is the Mean Value Theorem the bridge from local rates to whole-interval facts?

statement.p: A derivative at a point is local. Claims such as increasing on an interval or constant on an interval compare values. In your own words, why does the Mean Value Theorem make that leap, and what hypotheses must travel with it?

hint.p: Some instantaneous rate equals the average rate. If every instantaneous rate is positive, or zero, the corresponding net change is forced.

exercise.title: Why are critical numbers and zeros of f'' candidates rather than conclusions?

statement.p: f'(c)=0 need not be an extremum, and f''(c)=0 need not be an inflection point. In your own words, what extra evidence turns a candidate into a conclusion, and why is that warning the same idea in two different disguises?

hint.p: Look for an actual change: a sign change of f' for extrema, a sign change of f'' for inflection.

exercise.title: Why must every theorem in this chapter be used as a hypotheses-to-conclusion package?

statement.p: Fermat, Rolle, the Mean Value Theorem, the second derivative test, and l’Hospital’s Rule each fail when a hypothesis is dropped. In your own words, why is checking hypotheses part of using the theorem, rather than an optional courtesy after the conclusion is written?

hint.p: If the hypotheses are missing, the conclusion may still be true by luck. But the theorem is no longer the reason.

subsection.title: Where this points
subsection.p: This chapter taught us how to read a graph from its derivatives. That is already useful: we can locate peaks, valleys, flat points, bends, and asymptotes.
But many real questions do not start by asking for a graph. They ask for a choice.
subsection.md: \text{How fast is one quantity changing when another quantity is changing?}
subsection.p: Those questions still use derivatives, but now the graph is only part of the story. The next chapter turns shape information into decisions: related rates, optimization, and models. \label{sec:ch6-discovery}
